transcription.tex: We saw with in order to model something with a Binomial Distribution, we had to make some assumptions, e.g. each event was independent, and had two outcomes.\par We have similar restrictions on events for a Poisson Distribution:
Events occur singly in time. Treat arrivals as instantaneous.
The number of events in disjoint intervals is independent. An arrival just now does not change the chance of another arrival in the next interval.
The expected count is proportional to the interval length. The word “rate” is a clue in exam questions. Check that the assumptions fit the situation.

A website receives hits at a rate of 300 per hour.
(a) State a distribution that is suitable to model the number of hits obtained during a 1 minute interval.
(b) State two reasons for your answer to part (a).
Jan 2012 Q4
In one minute the mean is \(300/60=5\). Use \(X\sim\operatorname{Po}(5)\).
Hits occur singly, independently and at a constant rate. Any two of these properties justify the model.

parts.text: Given these restrictions, which of the following could we model using a Poisson Distribution (where any reasonable simplifying assumptions are justifiable)
A volcano erupts every 1000 years, and we’re interested in the probability of at least one eruption next year.
If a volcano erupted today and then finished erupting, it’s less likely to erupt next year. So events are not independent.
On average the 281 bus comes 10 times an hour. We’re interested in the probability of (at least one) bus coming in the next hour.
Definitely not. Buses aren’t equally likely to come at any moment – the probability is going to spike each 6 minutes since buses intend to come at regular intervals, not randomly.
A call centre receives on average 80 calls an hour, and wish to work out the probability they have over 100 calls at some hour in the day.
Yes, justified, provided that the average rate is constant. We’re making some simplifying assumptions, such as that we don’t have repeat calls from the same customer.

transcription.tex:
Defects occur at random in planks of wood with a constant rate of 0.5 per 10 cm length. Jim buys a plank of length 100 cm.
(a) Find the probability that Jim’s plank contains at most 3 defects.
Shivani buys 6 planks each of length 100 cm.
(b) Find the probability that fewer than 2 of Shivani’s planks contain at most 3 defects.
May 2011 Q5
The mean is 0.5 defects per 10 cm, hence 5 per plank. With \(X\sim\operatorname{Po}(5)\), \(P(X\le3)=0.2650\).
Let \(Y\) count the planks containing at most 3 defects. For six independent planks, \(Y\sim\operatorname{B}(6,0.2650)\).\par \(P(Y<2)=P(Y=0)+P(Y=1)\)\par \(=0.735^6+6(0.265)(0.735)^5=0.4987\ldots\).

Think carefully about whether we wish to use Binomial or Poisson. You should be clear about what your random variables are and how they’re distributed. Sometimes we need to scale the rate to a different time period/length.
